dram-vs-sram.title: DRAM vs SRAM: Key Differences Explained
dram-vs-sram.description: DRAM vs SRAM in one table: cell structure, refresh, speed, density, cost, power and typical uses, plus a guide to when each one is used.
dram-vs-sram.lead: DRAM stores each bit as charge on a tiny capacitor, so it is dense and cheap but must be refreshed. SRAM stores each bit in a latch built from transistors, so it is faster and needs no refresh, but takes much more area per bit. That is why computers use DRAM for large main memory and SRAM for small, fast caches.
rows: Storage element
One transistor and one capacitor (1T1C). The bit is the presence or absence of charge on the capacitor
Usually six transistors (6T): two cross-coupled inverters forming a latch, plus two access transistors
Refresh
Required. Charge leaks away, so every row must be read and rewritten periodically (typically within 64 ms)
Not required. The latch holds its data as long as power is applied
Without power
Data is lost (volatile)
Data is lost (volatile)
Area per bit
Small (a cell is about 6F², where F is the minimum feature size)
Large (an order of magnitude or more bigger than DRAM)
Speed
Slower. A row must be activated and later precharged, so an access takes tens of nanoseconds
Fast. On-chip SRAM can be accessed in about a nanosecond, a few clock cycles
Cost per bit
Low
High (because of the larger area)
Standby power
Needs refresh even when idle (reduced by self-refresh modes)
No refresh, but transistor leakage in a large array adds up
Manufacturing
Uses deep capacitor structures and high-k dielectric films, and is made in dedicated memory fabs
Built in a standard logic CMOS process, so it can sit on the same chip as the processor
Typical capacity
Several to tens of gigabits per chip
Kilobytes to tens of megabytes per cache level in a typical processor
Typical uses
Main memory (DDR, LPDDR) and graphics memory (GDDR, HBM)
CPU and GPU caches, register files and small on-chip buffers
when: When you need a lot of memory at a low cost per bit and can tolerate some latency: main memory in PCs, servers and smartphones, and graphics memory for GPUs.
When speed matters most and the capacity can be small: CPU caches, register files, and small buffers where you do not want refresh circuitry.
Real computers use both. A fast SRAM cache holds frequently used data and hides the latency of the slower DRAM.
